source.title: Natural Language Descriptions of Deep Visual Features
source.authors: Evan Hernandez; Sarah Schwettmann; David Bau; Teona Bagashvili; A. Torralba; Jacob Andreas

record.tranche_reason: The study uses MILAN descriptions of neurons' high-activation image regions to examine whether individual visual neurons correspond to multiple distinct concepts. This is a different measurement from the original feature-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The study gives examples of neurons described as detecting multiple concepts, including a ResNet18 neuron described as detecting animals, vehicles, and vases. It also reports ablation results for neurons grouped by caption properties. Generalization BERTScores, face-neuron counts, and text-neuron counts do not measure polysemanticity and are not included as rows. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: MILAN labels neurons in vision classifiers from their top-activating image regions. The paper scores captions for semantic incoherence (max word difference) and shows neurons whose descriptions join dissimilar concepts, such as ResNet18 layer4-427 ('animals, vehicles, and vases') and a 'dog faces and cupcakes' neuron. This bears on V1 through a method other than feature visualization. It is qualitative and a proxy: there is no prevalence estimate, and the word-difference grouping is a top-10% selection.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MILAN produces fine-grained neuron descriptions that agree with humans better than baselines, and that these support analysis, auditing and editing. They caution that the descriptions are partial and potentially noisy. On this claim specifically, they say neurons with dissimilar-concept descriptions appear less important and contribute to non-robust behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: MILAN generates descriptions by scoring natural-language captions against sets of high-activation image regions; the study does not reproduce the original feature-visualization procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron descriptions are based on sets of 15 top-activating images, with activation thresholds set at the 0.99 percentile. The study does not vary these choices to measure their effect on polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating neurons with high max-word-difference captions hurts ImageNet accuracy much less than ablating random neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons whose descriptions mix semantically dissimilar concepts are less important to classification accuracy than average neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: A cut-and-paste input aimed at a mixed-concept neuron makes the model predict an unrelated class (amphibian when a military vehicle is pasted).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons with mixed-concept descriptions can mediate non-robust predictions.

record.problems: The direct example is qualitative and does not establish how prevalent mixed-concept neurons are. The authors state that MILAN descriptions are partial and potentially noisy; the ablation comparison is reported qualitatively in the text without exact values or uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: How common mixed-concept neurons are in vision models; InceptionV1 and its specific neurons; confirming with feature visualization.
Not tested: no language models (the ViT MLP neurons are used only for description agreement).
Not tested: the share of polysemantic neurons is not compared across architectures or training choices.
Not tested: whether the mixed neurons share an underlying feature.
Not tested: exemplar settings (k=15, 0.99 percentile) and scoring are fixed and not varied.

missing.what: A neuron described as 'dog faces and cupcakes', presented as detecting perceptually similar but fundamentally different objects. MILAN's caption missed the cupcakes, so automated descriptions can under-report mixing.
missing.locator: Figure 2; Section 4 failure modes; Section 5 intro

missing.what: Layer distribution of neurons in the top 10% of word difference in ResNet18: neurons with large semantic differences are more prevalent in later layers.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. The evidence for V1 is indirect: 'polysemantic' here is operationalized as semantic distance between words in a generated caption, which depends on both the captioning model and spaCy word vectors. The study does not use the term polysemantic.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not estimate how common such neurons are across vision models, or examine the specific InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55.
Language models and transformer MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Whether activation function, architecture, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons, or whether that share can be lowered without a large performance loss.
The study does not test whether apparently mixed neurons share a feature or job that better tools reveal.
The study does not vary activation range or explanation-scoring method to test their effect on whether a neuron counts as polysemantic.

rows.subject: ResNet18-ImageNet layer4-427
rows.operation_detail: MILAN generated a description from the neuron's high-activation image exemplars.
rows.measure: Concepts represented in the generated neuron description and illustrated by exemplar images
rows.value: The neuron is described as detecting animals, vehicles, and vases.
rows.note: The authors use this neuron as an example of a description containing dissimilar concepts. The paper does not quantify how often neurons have this property.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The evidence is a single figure example (Fig. 13 / Fig. 14a), and the description is MILAN-generated, which the authors call partial and potentially noisy.

rows.subject: ResNet18-ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Cut and pasted an object into an image to test a neuron selected for a high maximum-word-difference description.

labels.reason: One neuron's MILAN description joins unrelated concepts (r1). Fig. 14 adds cut-and-paste evidence: pasting a vehicle makes the model predict amphibian. This is consistent with V1, but anecdotal, and the authors call the descriptions partial and potentially noisy.

relation.reason: Borderline. The paper's own results show a neuron whose description and adversarial behaviour join animals and vehicles (Figs. 13-14), and an ablation result for the max-word-diff group. These bear on V1 qualitatively.

tranche.reason: MILAN uses a different method (PMI-guided captions of top-activating regions, plus a cut-and-paste test in Fig. 14) and reports neurons that join dissimilar concepts. T2 fits, but the paper is mainly a tool paper and gives no prevalence.

source_check.notes: Evidence for V1 is a few hand-picked neurons: layer4-427 (Figs. 13-14) and a 'dog faces and cupcakes' neuron (Fig. 2) whose cupcakes MILAN misses. No row records the dog/cupcake neuron or the Fig. 14 cut-and-paste result. The paper gives no prevalence of polysemantic neurons, and the max-word-diff measure is caption-based.

statements.problem: None for this study. MILAN describes layer4-427 as 'animals, vehicles, and vases'. Section 3.1 gives k = 15 images and a 0.99-percentile threshold. Figure 13 examples come from the first 10 ablated neurons, so they are selected units with no prevalence.

None. The Figure 4 caption says neurons with large semantic differences are more prevalent in late layers of ResNet18. The measure is the top 10% max word difference in MILAN captions, not a direct polysemanticity score, and the text gives no numbers.

None. Section 5 says that when a caption contains highly dissimilar words, ablation hurts performance substantially less than ablating random neurons (ResNet18, ImageNet validation). No numbers are given.
